extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of science; readers of Bacon's Novum Organum; general readers interested in scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial footnotes and commentary on Bacon's Novum Organum discussing standards of scientific inquiry, induction, experiment design, and common pitfalls in reasoning. The page annotates the original aphorisms with methodological guidance and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective instances (use many particular cases to induce a law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The collective instances here meant are no other than general facts or laws of some degree of generality, and are themselves the result of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many particular phenomena presented together (e.g., the system of Jupiter or Saturn with satellites, parabolic jet form, figures on vibrating plates, colored lemniscates in crystals, Kepler's laws) as ocular evidence that suggests a general law; such collective instances materially assist in securing acceptance of broader systems (e.g., Copernican, Newtonian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective instances of ocular inspection (large simultaneous examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A species of collective instance in which particular phenomena are presented in such numbers at once as to make the induction of their law a matter of ocular inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek phenomena where many individual parts are seen together (jet of water showing particle trajectories; sand figures on vibrating plates) so the law emerges by inspection; these furnish advanced posts in philosophical exploration and can point directly to mathematical expressions of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crucial instances to decide between rival hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucial instances afford the readiest and securest means of eliminating extraneous causes, and deciding between the claims of rival hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments where competing theories predict different observable outcomes (decisive tests). Example: Fresnel's experiment on thin-film colors gave different predictions under competing theories of light and was decisive in favor of wave/vibration theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate possible causes and use dilemmas (but beware paralogisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In proposing to explain an effect, commence with enumeration of causes which seem connected with its production; then, with dilemmas, eliminate phenomena accidental to its composition and attribute the effect to the residue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elimination-by-dilemma as a method, but be aware of two principal paralogisms: false exclusions (omitting real causes) and defective enumerations (failing to list all possibilities). Always check for omitted causes (e.g., melting polar ice, thermal expansion) and for simultaneous influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty generalization / check counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Is not this very hasty generalization? (criticizing assertions that generalize from insufficient examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before generalizing, examine possible counterexamples and variations (e.g., count of serpent segments vs centipedes). Do not accept a universal statement from a small or unrepresentative sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments to reveal facts beyond the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific facts are elicited by instruments which sense alone could never have revealed (air-pump, barometer, measurement of light velocity, experiments in electricity and galvanism, pneumatic chemistry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ apparatus and quantitative instruments to detect and measure phenomena inaccessible to unaided senses; trust instrumental evidence when properly controlled and calibrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics/geometry are necessary to complete induction in many cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases the result of a number of particular facts, or the collective instances rising out of them, can only be discovered by geometry, which so far becomes necessary to complete the work of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experiments give values for many instances but not the general relation, apply deductive/mathematical analysis (e.g., law of refraction, Newton's derivation of rainbow breadth) to deduce the invariant relation linking variables; combine precise measurement with mathematical deduction to transform probable conjectures into certain facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain precise quantitative measurements across multiple relevant quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: It was necessary to determine with precision the demi-diameter of the earth, the velocity of falling bodies at its surface, the distance of the moon, and the speed with which she describes her orbit, before the relation could be discovered between terrestrial gravity and lunar motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect accurate, quantitative data for all relevant variables before inferring physical laws; insufficient or imprecise measurement across necessary dimensions can prevent discovery of real relations (e.g., gravitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek frontier/itinerant instances to detect continuity (natura non agit per saltum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The itinerant instances, as well as frontier instances, are cases in which we are enabled to trace the general law of continuity which seems to pervade all nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transitional cases (e.g., transparency vs opacity illustrated by gold-leaf) that show qualities are degrees on a continuum rather than strict opposites; such instances can reveal continuity laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conceptual categories clearly (avoid conflating distinct notions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author in the text confounds inertness, which is a simple indifference of bodies to action, with gravity, which is a force acting always in proportion to their density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and separate concepts (e.g., inertness vs gravity) carefully in argument and theory to avoid mistaken inferences; conceptual clarity prevents misattribution of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanistic/testable explanations over vague 'spirits' hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon introduces 'spirits' to explain phenomena he could not understand; such ad hoc hypotheses give the air of explanation but are unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resorting to vague, untestable entities to 'explain' phenomena; favor explanations that propose mechanisms amenable to empirical test and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments that exploit differences in predictions between theories
rubrics_metrics.description: When two theories are both applicable, note where they predict different circumstances (e.g., bright stripe intervals when using a prism) and perform the relevant observation to decide between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify concrete experimental conditions under which rival theories diverge, then carry out those observations (control for confounders) to obtain decisive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish reference standards/zeros when comparing magnitudes (e.g., heat vs cold)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to compare a degree of heat with a degree of cold without the assumption of some arbitrary test, to which the degrees are to be referred. The zero must be arbitrary which divides equally a certain degree of heat from a certain degree of cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define measurement scales and reference points explicitly before comparing intensities or magnitudes; choose and state the convention (zero) used for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in criticizing established theories; interpret terms consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: If Bacon's remark be accepted, the censure will fall upon Newton ... the centre of which Newton speaks is not a point with an active inherent force, but only the result of all the particular and reciprocal attractions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or criticizing established theories, ensure you understand and interpret their technical terms as intended by proponents; apparent contradictions may be due to misinterpretation rather than substantive error.
